translated_data.fullTranslation:
Chapter I, in which Phileas Fogg and Passepartout accept each other, the one as master, the other as servant. In the year 1872, the house numbered 7 on Saville Row, Burlington Gardens—the house in which Sheridan died in 1814—was occupied by Phileas Fogg, Esq., one of the most peculiar and most noticed members of the Reform Club of London, although he seemed to make a point of doing nothing that might attract attention. Thus one of the greatest orators who have honoured England was succeeded by this Phileas Fogg, an enigmatic figure about whom nothing was known, except that he was a thoroughly gallant man and one of the finest gentlemen of English high society.

It was said that he resembled Byron—in the head, for he was irreproachable as to the feet—but a Byron with a moustache and whiskers, an impassive Byron, who might have lived a thousand years without growing old.

English he certainly was, but Phileas Fogg was perhaps not a Londoner. He had never been seen at the Stock Exchange, nor at the Bank, nor in any of the counting-houses of the City. Neither the basins nor the docks of London had ever received a ship whose owner was Phileas Fogg. This gentleman sat on no board of directors. His name had never resounded in a college of barristers, neither at the Temple, nor at Lincoln's Inn, nor at Gray's Inn. He never pleaded in the Court of Chancery, nor in the Queen's Bench, nor in the Exchequer, nor in the Ecclesiastical Court. He was neither a manufacturer, nor a trader, nor a merchant, nor a farmer. A London club founded in 1836 (corpus note).
